NPDev capabilities catalogue

Everything the model language can say, one row per keyword. A keyword is a word you may write in a model file, such as maxLength on a field or runAs on a flow. This page shows, for each one, what it does, whether the platform really implements it, whether the official samples use it, whether a test covers it, a real example, and why it exists.

How to read this page

Each row is one keyword. Click a row to open it: you get the plain explanation, the type of value it takes, a real example copied from an official sample, the tests and code that mention it, and the written reason it was admitted to the language.

Implemented
What the platform really does with the word, judged by which parts of the code name it. The model passes through a pipeline: the parser reads the JSON, plumbing classes (the syntax tree, the compiled model, the resolver, the compiled-model writers) copy a value along without looking at it, validators check it, other build-time classes act on it while the model is built, and the generator, kernel, runtime host and UI act on it when the app runs. Code is found by name, through quoted keys and through accessor calls such as flow.expose().
runs the generator, kernel, runtime or UI acts on it. builds it acts while the model is parsed, resolved or compiled. tooling only the command line or AI tooling names it. validated only and plumbing only only a validator, or only the parser and the compiled-model plumbing, name it: no code was found that acts on the value (code using it under another name would not show here, so confirm before removing). ignored no code names it at all: the schema accepts it and the value is dropped. file key a structural key such as $ref.
Official samples
How many official models use it. Official means the models that exist to show or pin the language (roles showcase, canary and dsl-fixture in the corpus list) and the built-in packs. Each model is walked against the schema, so a word that appears in many places is credited only where it truly belongs. Use in repro cases and engine variants is shown in the detail, but does not count.
Real models
How many of those official models are real apps and packs, leaving out dsl-conformance-max. That model is the coverage fixture: it exists to touch every word once, so it proves a word can be written, not that anyone needs it. 0 means only the fixture uses the word.
Tested
How many test files mention it. This is by name; the badge shared means other keywords have the same name, so the evidence cannot say which one it proves.
Corpus
It is used in dsl-conformance-max, the model the build gate generates every time.
Example
A real JSON example exists: from an official sample when one uses the word, otherwise from the reference example of its definition.
Story
A short story in everyday words: a real situation, the problem it causes, and what the keyword does about it. It is written so that someone who has never programmed can hold on to the idea.
Justified
A written admission record explains why the language needs this word (declarative, not expressible lower, used twice, enforced, taught). Older keywords predate that rule, so most show none yet: that is the work list.
Status
complete means all six pieces exist (code, sample, test, example, story, written reason). Otherwise it lists what is missing. unused marks a candidate for removal: no official sample and no test.

The language is meant to stay small. When a need is rare, the right answer is usually code the author writes (a function, a flow step, a JavaScript page or a Java class) and not one more keyword. Use the filters to find keywords that no sample, test or reason supports.
